title: Stop Writing Tone Instructions. Layer Them. - Isadora Martin-Dye, Isadora & Co
talk_summary: A wedding-venue operator describes replacing 24 scattered system prompts with a single four-layer prompt assembler: immutable identity rules, situational mode from user context, example-anchored voice, and a deterministic post-generation veto. The core claim is that instructions are probabilistic requests while a post-generation check is deterministic permission, and that guarantees (dates, prices, identity) must be enforced by the latter.

takeaways.technique: Deterministic post-generation veto as a shared gate
takeaways.what_they_do: After the LLM produces output, a cheap non-LLM check reads the actual text and rejects it if it violates hard constraints (e.g., offered dates not in an allow-list), rather than trusting prompt instructions to prevent it.

takeaways.technique: Single canonical prompt assembler with fixed layer order
takeaways.what_they_do: All surfaces compose their system prompt through one entry point in a fixed order (hard rules first, task last), replacing 24 ad hoc prompts; ordering is treated as load-bearing.

takeaways.technique: Render soft human context before numeric constraints
takeaways.what_they_do: The assembler deliberately places qualitative context notes before numeric guard blocks so the model sets tone/framing first, then satisfies numbers, avoiding mechanically slotted prose.
takeaways.evidence_quote: Couple note block render before the numbers guard block... Reversing the order makes the prose feel mechanically slotted

takeaways.technique: Fail-loud on missing tenant identity, never default
takeaways.what_they_do: In a multi-tenant system, missing brand identity fields throw an error instead of silently defaulting, after a leak where every venue shipped as the same sender identity.
takeaways.evidence_quote: In a multi-tenant system, identity must never have a default. A missing brand identity is a crash, not a fallback.

takeaways.technique: Asymmetric soft-flag vs hard-reject veto tiers
takeaways.what_they_do: Two veto types: a soft flag that logs/flags suspicious output for human double-check, and a hard reject for expensive failures (fabricated numbers). Explicitly reasons about false-positive vs false-negative cost asymmetry.
takeaways.evidence_quote: A false positive means someone double-checked a phone response. A false negative remains a hallucinated number or a privacy violation that ships to a client.

takeaways.technique: Prefer deterministic pattern rejects over a classifier for vetoes
takeaways.what_they_do: Chose fast deterministic pattern matching for the veto layer over a small probabilistic classifier, accepting lower coverage for guaranteed correctness on covered patterns.
takeaways.evidence_quote: rejects is fast and cheap and deterministic. It either matches or it doesn't... right now I'm choosing determinism over coverage.
